study.name: Is the whole the sum of its parts? Neural computation of consumer bundle valuation in humans
study.citation: Cross, L., Webb, R., & O'Doherty, J. P. (2026). Is the whole the sum of its parts? Neural computation of consumer bundle valuation in humans. The Journal of Neuroscience, 46(2), e0983252025. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0983-25.2025
study.description: Deep-fMRI study; behavioural data at github.com/locross93/Bundle_Value, imaging at OSF hxa9p.

description: Willingness-to-pay for single items, elicited in an incentive-compatible Becker-DeGroot-Marschak auction outside the scanner on each of three days. Participants held a $20 cash endowment and bid $0-20 for each item, knowing one trial would be drawn and played for real. Each participant saw 40 of the 110 items: 20 per day, half food and half non-comestible consumer goods, with 10 items carried across all three days and 10 new ones introduced each day. Those carried items give three timepoints; items seen on a single day have timepoint 1. Bids on two-item bundles, which make up most of the experiment, are not held here because this database is item-level. Item names were resolved from the numeric stimulus indices in the authors' analysis repository against Tables S1 and S2 of the paper. Which table an index belongs to is fixed by the data: indices 1-70 are the food table and 101-140 the consumer table, and that split reproduces the paper's stated design of 10 food and 10 non-food items on every one of the 42 participant-days. That an index equals its row number within a table is an inference from the tables being numbered 1-70 and 1-40 to match; it is supported by 55 of the 56 food items of Suzuki et al. (2017) appearing in Table S1, and by substantial prepared foods attracting the highest bids and small packaged snacks the lowest, but it was not confirmed by the authors.
